blocks.text: That's all for now!
Thank you for participating in our latest live conversation ahead of the November US midterm elections.

We’ve been hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms, and we’ll be back with one more conversation before US voters head to the polls – this time on how immigration policies and ICE have been shaping America.

Join us on 22 October at 12pm ET for a conversation with immigration reporters Maanvi Singh and José Olivares, along with Los Angeles correspondent Sam Levin, will take your questions. Send us your questions.
To keep up with our coverage of the midterms sign up to the Stakes newsletter here and bookmark our US midterm elections page.
Why are prices so high? Stateside shares more
The vast majority of Americans say they are struggling to pay for gas and groceries, and are cutting back on luxuries.
Today, Stateside podcast hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman published an episode with Guardian columnist and former labor secretary Robert Reich explaining why readers may be feeling the pinch.

From breaking down the market factors behind the cost of a $16 cheesesteak, to explaining why AI is playing into the price of a Nintendo Switch 2, Reich reveals who you should point the finger at in this economy. Watch it here.
What is your personal ‘recession indicator’?
Nearly two-thirds of Americans think the US is experiencing a recession, according to a new Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian.

We want to hear from Americans: do you feel like the US is experiencing a recession? What is your so-called personal “recession indicator”, or a signal in your everyday life that points to an incoming economic slump? Tell us about your experience in the form below.
How will the rising interest rates affect an already challenging housing market?
Kathleen OKeefe, Ringwood, NJ asks in a callout question: How will the rising interest rates affect an already challenging housing market?

double quotation markLauren: Interest rates have a direct impact on mortgage rates and other loans as it defines how much it costs to borrow money. At the beginning of the pandemic, the US Federal Reserve set interest rates to zero, bringing mortgage rates down to historic lows.This is why we saw a surge of activity in the housing market from 2020 to 2022. At the end of that period, the Fed started to bring interest rates up, bringing mortgage rates to the averages that we see today (over 7% for a 30-year mortgage). This has brought the housing market to a standstill, and even though interest rates are still lower than its most recent peak in 2023, mortgage rates haven’t really come down all that much. It was only this past February that the rate for a 30-year mortgage went below 6% for the first time since September 2022, and it’s only kept climbing.

blocks.caption: A residential development in Des Moines, Iowa. Photograph: Aerial Archives/Alamy

blocks.text: How is Trump faring with independent voters after two years?

FetchCB001 asks: US politics is so polarised, you have a group who will always vote Republican regardless and a group who will never regardless. This tends to mean that elections are decided by the floaters. Is there any indication of how these voters have been impacted by the first two years of Trump 2?

double quotation markMichael: Approval from independent voters for Trump’s presidency has declined throughout his second term; 43% of independent voters supported him during his presidential campaign in 2024. By April 2026, that support declined to 26%. A September 2026 YouGov survey found that 23% of independents approve of Trump, compared with 79% of Republicans and 2% of Democrats. A September poll conducted by Fox News found 73% saying Trump has made the economy worse, compared to 95% of Democrats and 26% of Republicans.

blocks.caption: Voters wait for polling station to open on the first day of early voting in North CarolinaVoters wait for a polling station to open on the first day of early voting in the state, in Raleigh, North Carolina, US, October 15, 2026. Photograph: Jonathan Drake/Reuters

blocks.text: double quotation markGaya: Our polling with Harris earlier this summer captured the angst and frustration that rural American voters are feeling in today’s economy, often more so than their urban and suburban counterparts. Here’s what we found about rural voters : - 70% say that the federal government has made the affordability crisis either significantly or somewhat worse in 2026 - 64% believe that the national economy is getting worse; 57% believe that their local economy is getting worse - Nearly half believe that their financial security is getting worse - 46% say they are just getting by, while 29% say they are struggling to make ends meet - 57% say they have trouble affording groceries, compared to 55% and 47% of urban and suburban voters
How seriously does Trump's base take his promises of cash if he wins the midterms?

Mr_202: I’d love to know how seriously Trump’s base take his promises of bribes and sunny uplands. The DOGE cheques, the tariff rebates, the cheques in the post if he wins the midterms. Do these people honestly believe the money will come and if not, do they care that it’s being promised? Do they think they’re getting half price, commandeered Venezuelan oil any time soon? Thank you for your attention to this matter and keep bringing the cold hard truths.

double quotation markHeather: About one million Americans should start seeing checks of about $500 each related to what the White House called Obamacare refunds before they go to the polls. (Some reports suggest that money is coming from funds previously used to support healthcare signup and the website that it uses.) Trump has also promised 20 million seniors a $90 check for Medicare fees. These appear to be happening, but the promised DOGE and tariffs rebates, as you note, never did. It’s unclear how he would fund a promise to give voters $5,000 after the midterms if Republicans win, especially because few lawmakers in his party have publicly supported that idea. While it’s hard to evaluate where the diehard “Forever Trumpers” are on believing what the President says, Republicans’ optimism about the economy overall has taken a nosedive. In February 2025, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better and by February 2026 that optimism was up to 49%. In our latest Harris poll, that number dropped to 28%.

blocks.caption: President  Trump speaks at the Republican convention in Dallas on 9 September. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP

blocks.text: Which utility has seen the biggest surge under Trump?
From an Instagram user: What utility has seen the biggest surge in pricing since 2nd Trump administration?

double quotation markGaya: We can answer this by looking at data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Utility gas services increased at an annual rate of 5% this month, slightly more than the 4.4% increase in electricity. Last year, in Trump’s first September in office, gas services had increased by 11.7% compared to the year before, while electricity increased by 5.1%. Looking more broadly at energy commodities — which don’t necessarily show up as a monthly bill, but can still affect overall household expenses — we can see that fuel oil, which is used to heat homes and offices, increased by 74.2% compared to the year before. (In comparison, fuel oil had increased by just 4.1% in the September 2025 report).
Do lower-income Americans tend to vote Republican?

Grauniad9999: A question my 16-year-old asked me that I couldn’t answer well. Why is support for conservative parties in the UK mostly comprised of the well-off, where in the US the equivalent is mostly supported by poorer, non-college folks?

double quotation markMichael: I think that’s more perception than reality, especially as the Democratic Party has been grappling with criticism of losing working class support, while Republicans and the Trump administration have pushed narratives that working class, including union members have been increasingly supportive of Trump, but that is not the case based on exit polls. Pew Research found in 2024 that lower income, lower middle income, and high income voters leaned Democrat, while upper middle and middle income voters leaned Republican.

blocks.caption: The crowd cheers after the 2024 presidential election is called for Donald Trump on 6 November 2024. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters

blocks.text: Politicians say the US economy is growing - is it actually?
Clifford Weiler, San Diego, CA asks in a callout question: Politicians cite how the economy is improving, but how is the rising rate of inflation taken into account?

double quotation markLauren: What growth in the economy means really depends on who you’re talking to. For economists, economic growth is measured by gross domestic product (GDP), which is an equation adding together consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. A little inflation can actually stimulate further growth, as long as it doesn’t lead to a pullback in spending. That’s why the US Federal Reserve’s target inflation rate is 2% (something that hasn’t been seen since January 2021 – for context, it was 3.7% in September). For both economists and politicians, inflation really only becomes a bad thing when it starts to impact consumer spending. When prices get too high and consumers start spending less money, the wheels of the economy can start to slow. Even though inflation has been high, and consumers are anxious about the economy, we haven’t yet seen a large pullback in spending that would cause alarm over growth.

blocks.caption: Shoppers shop at a grocery store in Glenview, IL October 2026. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP

blocks.text: double quotation markLauren continues: For many goods and services, economists actually think prices going down as a bad thing for the overall economy that can trigger a downtown. There are some major exceptions, energy prices being a big one. If the US and Iran ever reach a peace deal, and oil transportation and reduction goes back to normal, gas prices will go down. This is what we saw in 2022, once the energy market recalibrated for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. After high periods of inflation, certain food prices can also go down. The cost of eggs is about 20% lower than they were a year ago, when prices were high because of avian-flu related shortages. For both economists and politicians, inflation really only becomes a bad thing when it starts to impact consumer spending. When prices get too high and consumers start spending less money, the wheels of the economy can start to slow. Even though inflation has been high, and consumers are anxious about the economy, we haven’t yet seen a large pullback in spending that would cause alarm over growth.
Are moderate Republican candidates distancing themselves from Trump in the face of his unpopular policies?

NorthLondonIsRed asks: For years, more moderate Republicans seemed to have little choice but to align with Trump to win their primaries and general elections. With the Iran war and rising prices straining many voters, could the incentives now flip, so that distancing themselves from Trump becomes the safer path in November? And are any Republicans already making that calculation?

double quotation markMichael: Yes, there have been several Republican candidates who have attempted to distance themselves from Trump, given his low approval ratings that have been in the 30s. In September, Republican Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar released an ad saying Trump’s immigration policies have gone too far. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said in the ad. In California, Republican Congresswoman Young Kim has dropped references to Trump from her campaign website and digital materials, as she faces a tight re-election battle. Other candidates have removed mentions of focuses of Trump from campaign websites, such as Florida Republican Governor candidate Byron Donalds, but denied the changes were a dig at Trump.

double quotation markHeather: Another place we’re seeing some Republicans break with Trump is on tariffs, which is a direct response to the anger over their impacts. Trump’s former VP Mike Pence (who is not running for anything, but still gets an ear in some Washington circles) has been the loudest voice on this in the party, and Michigan’s Mike Rogers recently issued an ad calling for an end to the tariff war with Canada.

blocks.caption: U.S. Representative Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL) speaks during a press conference regarding Cuba and the U.S. indictment of former Cuban President Raul Castro, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 20, 2026. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

articles.title: Texas sued after glitch delays almost 600,000 voter registrations
articles.summary:
Voting registration organizations accuse Texas officials of failing to ensure eligible voters can register properly

Texas election officials are struggling to process a massive backlog of…

blocks.text: Texas election officials are struggling to process a massive backlog of nearly 600,000 voter registration applications after a major state computer system failure, just days before early voting is set to open on Monday and amid concerns about widespread voter suppression.

The disruption has raised serious concerns about the state’s voter registration system, with voting rights organizations accusing Texas officials of failing to ensure that eligible voters could properly register.

The problem originated from a software error involving the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS), according to a lawsuit filed last week. The glitch affected a website used for driver’s license applications that was also designed to allow Texans to register to vote.

The lawsuit alleges that between October 2025 and February 2026, residents who selected “yes” when asked whether they wanted to register to vote were given receipts confirming their selections. However, their registration information was never actually recorded.
The League of Women Voters of Texas and Move Texas Civic Fund, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing civic participation among young Texans, brought the legal challenge against state officials.

“Defendants have breached and continue to breach the contract by failing to maintain the procedures that ensure simultaneous online voter registration with driver license renewal or change of address transactions,” the lawsuit said.

“DPS had failed to send almost 600,000 voter registrations to the SOS to distribute to local county registrars, with some delayed voter registrations stretching back as far as October 2025,” it added. “Unexpecting counties must now scramble to process this deluge of last-minute voter registrations ahead of the November 2026 election.”
Among those named in the complaint are Texas secretary of state Robert Howden, the state’s top election official, and DPS director Freeman F Martin.

The lawsuit demands that both agencies establish and maintain a working voter registration process. It also seeks records detailing registration failures and an order requiring officials to provide the court with evidence of compliance within one month.

The registration breakdown is drawing national attention as Texas prepares for one of the country’s most closely contested US Senate elections this year. Donald Trump chose Texas attorney general Ken Paxton to run against James Talarico, a political newcomer who Democrats hope will be able to flip Texas’s longtime red Senate seat to blue.

California Democratic senator Alex Padilla, ranking member of the Senate rules committee, which has oversight of federal elections, demanded answers about the voting registration system from Texas leaders last month.
In a letter addressed to state governor Greg Abbott and Howden, Padilla pressed for an explanation of how the failure occurred and how many registrations were affected.

The controversy comes as voting rights advocates continue to warn about what they describe as broader efforts by the Trump administration to suppress voter participation. Those concerns include bids to rig electoral maps and threats to deploy federal law enforcement at polling sites, among other actions.

articles.title: UK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about it?
articles.summary:
Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key

Women in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could…

blocks.text: Women in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could persist for weeks. We take a look at the situation.
What is HRT?
Hormone replacement therapy is widely used to help women manage symptoms of menopause. It can take many forms, from gels and sprays to patches, pills, creams and intrauterine systems.

As the NHS notes, HRT typically involves two hormones – oestrogen and progestogen – and replaces levels lost as women go through menopause. These can be given separately or in a single type of HRT. Women who have had a hysterectomy only require oestrogen-containing HRT.

According to the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA), almost 2 million women in England aged 40 and above were prescribed HRT for menopause symptoms in 2025-26. Experts, however, say that access varies and shortages have been a problem.
Which items are affected by the current shortages?

According to a medicine supply notification issued by the Department of Health and Social Care this week, FemSeven Conti patches are out of stock and are expected to remain so until late November. The patches contain estradiol – a type of oestrogen– and a synthetic progestogen called levonorgestrel.
There are also shortages of various Estradot patches – a type of HRT that contains estradiol – and the situation is not expected to end until January.
This is not the first time there have been HRT shortages, and the supply issues affecting Estradot have been long-lasting. The shortages of some products began in December 2024, according to NHSBSA.

“When you have found an HRT treatment that helps you sleep, manage hot flushes and feel more like yourself, being told it is unavailable can be unsettling,” said Sobia Qasim, a pharmacist at the online pharmacy Curely.

Sehar Shahid, a member of the National Pharmacy Association’s board, also raised concerns. “We are deeply frustrated and concerned by shortages to a number of HRT products, with shortages of Estradot being the second longest running individual medicine shortage in the UK,” she said.
“Certain HRT products are specialised and cannot always be easily substituted for an alternative.”
What alternatives are there?

According to the FemSeven Conti notification, alternative patches include Evorel Conti, Estradot Conti 30/95 and Estradot Conti 40/130. These contain estradiol and a different type of synthetic progestogen called norethisterone, and are used twice rather than once a week.

Paula Briggs, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health and a former chair of the British Menopause Society, said keeping the same dose of estradiol was the important aspect. “They have different progestogens, but I do not think that that would have any adverse impact on symptom control,” she said, noting progestogens are required to protect the lining of the womb rather than manage symptoms.

Serious shortage protocols for the Estradot products also list alternatives, such as estradiol-containing patches by Estraderm MX and Evorel. “If we’re using the same dose of oestrogen delivered in a similar patch through the skin, really there is no need to worry,” said Briggs.
What should women do if they are affected by the shortages?

Shahid said people who had experienced disruption to their usual HRT regime should speak to their clinician, while Qasim cautioned against leaving a patch on for longer than prescribed, cutting patches up or borrowing HRT treatments from others.
What needs to happen next?
Briggs said shortages were likely to occur in the future “because year on year we’re seeing a more than 10% increase in use”, she said.
Shahid urged the government to take action. “The new secretary of state should convene a taskforce to fully grasp this issue, bringing together all aspects of the supply chain,” she said.

Houthis strike Yemen government palace in Aden

blocks.caption: Yemen's internationally recognized government is located in Aden [FILE DECEMBER 2025]Image: Saleh Al-Obeidi/AFP

blocks.text: Houthi rebels on Thursday said a missile attack targeted the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden.

Witnesses cited by news agencies reported several explosions and smoke rising from the area around the al-Maashiq Palace, in a rare attack on the headquarters of Yemen's internationally recognized government in the southern port city.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and members of the government were safe, according to Yemen's Information Ministry.
The ministry statement added two members of the prime minister's security detail were killed.
Other reports, citing government officials, said 10 people were injured. It is currently unclear if the palace itself was hit, or what the extent of damage could be.
Houthi-affiliated media reported the strikes targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya ​Saree said the strikes targeted what he called "Saudi ‌military operations headquarters in Aden," Reuters reported.

Yemen's civil war reignited in September as the Iran-backed Houthis launched a rapid offensive against government forces, capturing key territory along the Red Sea coast and expanding their control over swathes of territory on the Red Sea.
Since then both sides have regularly traded strikes. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, with several killed in separate attacks on Riyadh airport.
Despite, Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and government counter-offensives, the group’s recent territorial gains have largely remained intact.

articles.title: Carney says Albertans should vote ‘No to the Nine’ in referendum

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre, meets and greets volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Mike Sturk/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans should vote against the nine referendum questions focused on immigration and constitutional reform as he visited Calgary on Thursday.
Prominent campaign has urged residents to reject immigration, constitutional questions
“I just wanted to come here, thank you for what you’ve already done, thank you what you’re going to do in the next few days,” Carney told the crowd in the city's northeast.
“Make sure everyone’s out there marking their ballots ... including, ‘No to the Nine.’”
“No to the Nine” is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine ballot questions on Oct. 19, in addition to voting to remain in Canada.

items: Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?

blocks.text: Carney was meeting with volunteers and others at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary.
Earlier, he appeared to discuss the campaign with a person holding a sign tied to a campaign from Public Interest Alberta, an education advocacy group.
“‘No on the Nine’ … that’s good,” Carney said.
Carney says 'No to the 9' while campaigning for Canadian unity in Calgary

The prime minister has previously spoken out on the separatism question. In a Thanksgiving message delivered from a classroom in Edmonton, Carney highlighted various federal initiatives, such as the Pacific Link pipeline.
“We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines,” Carney said.

Carney is scheduled to join former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for his "Forever Canadian" group later today, while Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver a pro-unity message at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Friday.
Carney is also expected to attend rallies on Friday in Edmonton and Red Deer.

items: Carney, Poilievre bring federalist push to Alberta ahead of referendum vote
Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum

blocks.text: Volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park hold placards for Alberta's referendum during a visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, while saying she has voted to remain in Canada, has advocated for Albertans to vote yes on the other nine questions.
Speaking to CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault during a one-on-one interview in Calgary last week, Smith said the nine questions are those which she “wants a mandate” on.
“I haven’t been neutral on that,” Smith said. “I’ve been persuading people that this is what we need to do.”
Earlier this week, three former Alberta premiers urged voters to say “no” to the five immigration-related questions on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot.
CBC News has requested additional comment from the Prime Minister’s Office and a spokesperson for Smith.
Liberal MP says he's voting against questions
Liberal MP Corey Hogan, who represents a Calgary riding, spoke to the Calgary Eyeopener on Thursday about the nine other questions.
Hogan said he was voting “no” to the entire process.
“We should be asking ourselves, do we want to reward this kind of behaviour? And I don’t think that we should,” Hogan said.
“I don’t think that we should use our country as a bargaining chip … I think the questions are quite manipulative, they’re written in ways to get certain answers.”
LISTEN | Liberal MP Corey Hogan talks to the Calgary Eyeopener ahead of the referendum:
Calgary Eyeopener10:05Referendum 2026: Corey Hogan
Although he said he’d vote “no” to all nine questions as a sort of protest to the process, he was more open to ballot question seven, which involves abolishing the federal Senate.
“With all love to my senator colleagues, I love senators, I don’t love the Senate,” he said.

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast
articles.summary:
Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’

Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two…

blocks.text: Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea ⁠coast, setting them ablaze and raising ⁠fresh security concerns on a ​vital shipping route used by Ukraine.

A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came from Russia. “The drones that caused ⁠the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said.

Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the situation in the Black Sea as serious. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk,” he wrote on X. “Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.”

His statement followed a meeting with Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, and Nato’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, on Thursday, where they agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”, Dan said.
Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
A Nato official said the issue would be discussed at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council next week.

The missing crew were from the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged tanker travelling from Tunisia to Romania. All crew on the Yara J, which was struck just inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday, were safe.
Similar incidents in recent weeks have raised fears that the zone is becoming another front in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether Russia was responsible.

Romania shares a 614km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. The country has experienced frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including a daytime encroachment last November that led Nato to scramble fighter jets.
after newsletter promotion

EU leaders were already concerned about drone strikes on merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations, with 11 crew member from the HS Dignity, a cargo ship sailing under a Guinea-Bissau flag, still missing.

On another ship, the Ukrainian-operated Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.
“The results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians,” Radev said after arriving in Brussels for an EU summit on Thursday.
At least 23 sailors have been reported missing or killed after attacks on commercial shipping near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania in the past 10 days, according to Reuters.

Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on Ukraine’s Black Sea infrastructure, forcing Kyiv to turn to Danube river ports and Black Sea routes off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria to export its grain, sunflower oil and other products.

According to a draft summit declaration, EU leaders will say that attacks against civilian shipping, including “member state-flagged vessels, such as the recent attacks in Bulgaria’s and Romania’s exclusive economic zones in the Black Sea, are unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law”.

articles.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
articles.summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.

blocks.text: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".

He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.

Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

articles.title: Thames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027
articles.summary:
Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more money

Thames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water…

blocks.text: Thames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water company comes close to running out of cash.

The UK’s largest water company said on Thursday it needed another short-term cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its giant debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.

Thames Water said in a statement to the stock market that it “does not expect to complete its recapitalisation process ahead of this date”, meaning it would run out of cash without creditors stumping up more.

The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley. However, it has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.

The creditors gave Thames a £3bn lifeline in February last year to try to see it through negotiations on a deal to cut its debts and inject more money. The creditors, collectively called the London & Valley Water company, are led by a group of American hedge funds such as Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, and institutional investors including BlackRock and M&G.

However, those talks have dragged on, and the water company has now drawn down £2.65bn of the £3bn, leaving it perilously close to running out of cash even as it carries out a series of expensive repairs and upgrades.
Thames said the extra cash would “extend […] liquidity into autumn 2027 and allow [it] to continue to deliver its capital programme and deliver improvements for customers and the environment”.

Thames Water’s creditors have drawn up detailed proposals for a rescue plan that would involve them writing off £9.6bn in loans. However, that plan hinges on Ofwat agreeing to let the company pay set penalties for several years upfront, and effectively creating a special regime for the company. That prospect has proven politically unpalatable for the Labour government.

Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners called on Keir Starmer and then Andy Burnham to put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.
Burnham has pledged more public control of the UK’s water industry, and has said that public ownership for Thames Water “is what should be done”.
after newsletter promotion

In addition, the change of prime minister has led to regulatory uncertainty for the broader water industry. Starmer’s government had committed to implementing recommendations on changes to the water system from the former Bank of England deputy governor Sir John Cunliffe, but Burnham’s government has not yet made clear what it plans to do.
Thames Water said it “continues to work closely with stakeholders to secure a market-led solution”.
Thames Water’s creditors are expected to vote on the proposals later in the month.

articles.title: FBI investigates letters with ‘unknown substance’ sent to US election officials
articles.summary:
Election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma receive a powdery substance, prompting evacuations

The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials…

blocks.text: The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance”.

Just weeks before November’s US midterm elections, election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma received envelopes containing a powdery substance, leading to evacuations. A similar package containing white powder was also sent to the Ohio secretary of state, but the US Postal Service intercepted the package.

The US Senate sergeant at arms, who serves as chief law enforcement for the Senate, informed members of the upper chamber on Thursday of the investigation in a message, obtained by the Associated Press.

The notice said law enforcement officials were working to intercept additional mail, but it is possible some could reach their destination. Federal authorities have urged recipients to treat the mail as “potentially hazardous”.

Brendan Donahue, a senior official with the US Postal Inspection Service, confirmed the investigation into the suspicious mailings during a press conference on Thursday. “We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue said.
The US Postal Inspection Service referred the Guardian to the FBI.

In a statement, the FBI said it would not confirm specific instances but said that it was “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State office and their related election officers” alongside the US Postal Inspection Service.

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the FBI said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
The FBI declined to comment on what the purported substance may have been.
In Oklahoma, state troopers determined the substance mailed to the Oklahoma State Capitol complex was non-hazardous.
Two organizations representing secretaries of state and state election directors released a joint statement raising alarm at the mail containing the unknown substance.

The National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) “are deeply concerned by these incidents”, the organizations wrote in a statement on Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy,” they wrote. “Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties.”

Similar incidents have arisen during election cycles in the country. During the 2024 election, at least 14 election offices across the country had received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the substance turned out to be flour.
In 2023, election offices in six states also received mail containing white powder. In some cases, the powder contained trace amounts of fentanyl, a powerful opioid.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
articles.summary: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.

blocks.text: Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.
The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.
Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.
The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.

In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.
Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me."
"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.
Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.
"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.
Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.
The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.
The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.
Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.

Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
articles.summary: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski blamed his kidnapping for the fact he's currently representing himself at his fraud and money laundering trial in a victim impact statement he read at the…

image.caption: Self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski, seen before entering court last week, read his victim impact statement at the sentencing submissions hearing for his kidnapper in Superior Court in Toronto on Thursday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski blamed his kidnapping for the fact he's currently representing himself at his fraud and money laundering trial in a victim impact statement he read at the sentencing submissions for his kidnapper in Superior Court in Toronto on Thursday.
Aiden Pleterski read his victim impact statement in sentencing of kidnapper Thursday

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski blamed his kidnapping for the fact he's currently representing himself at his own trial in a victim impact statement he read at the sentencing submissions hearing for his kidnapper on Thursday.

"I have had to forego any normal routines, like having a steady job, as a safety precaution, which has spiralled into significant financial difficulties which have had far reaching consequences," said Pleterski in Superior Court in Toronto.
"The most significant is my inability to pay for a lawyer to defend me against the false allegations that this individual and others have made against me."

Pleterski's jury trial is currently underway in the same courthouse. He's pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. So far Pleterski has only cross-examined the first of a dozen witnesses called by the Crown.

items: Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest
'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist

blocks.text: Deren Akyeam-Pong pleaded guilty to nine charges related to Pleterski's 2022 kidnapping in October of last year. Those charges include kidnapping, assault and various gun charges.
This photo of Pleterski during his December 2022 kidnapping was entered as an exhibit during the guilty plea of his kidnapper Deren Akyeam-Pong. (Ontario Superior Court)

Pleterski, now 27, thought he was meeting with a potential investor on Dec. 5, 2022, when a gun was pressed into his ribs in the backseat of a pickup truck in Toronto. The abduction was the beginning of a three-day-long kidnapping during which Pleterski was threatened and tortured.

The torture included waterboarding, cigarette burns and getting beaten with golf clubs as his captors drove him between several locations in southern Ontario, according to the agreed statement of facts from Akyeam-Pong's guilty plea.
Three other men have also been charged in Pleterski's kidnapping. Their trial is expected to start later this year.
'Cannot sleep at night': Pleterski
"The thought that I may soon end up sharing a jail cell with my kidnappers has completely debilitated my ability to think clearly through this," read Pleterski in court Thursday.

"I cannot sleep at night. I come to court alone and am being asked to represent myself, but all I think about is being locked in a prison for an extended period of time with the same people who kidnapped, beat and threatened me."
Pleterski also spoke about the "emotional consequences" of his kidnapping, which he said are "difficult to explain to those who have not lived through it."
"Fear, stress, uncertainty and the continuing effort to process what happened consumes my thoughts and affects my well-being on a continuous basis."
The Crown in Pleterski's fraud and money laundering trial is alleging he spent investor money on himself, including on flights on private jets. (aiden_pletersik/Instagram)

The Crown in Pleterski's trial is alleging he guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski spent investors' money on exotic cars, private jet flights: Crown

blocks.text: "Whatever opinions people may have of me, my financial affairs or the circumstances that preceded these events, no financial dispute justifies kidnapping, violence or intimidation," Pleterski said in his victim impact statement.

"Ultimately, I want to be able to move forward with my life without being defined by these events. I just hope that the time will come that I don't have to look over my shoulder or worry about the safety of my family."

Tracey Vogel, the Crown prosecutor in the kidnapping sentencing, is asking for a 23-year sentence for Akyeam-Pong related to the kidnapping conviction and a separate conviction for eight gun and drug-related offences.
Craig Zeeh, Akyeam-Pong's lawyer, is asking for a 12-year sentence. Sentencing submissions are expected to continue Thursday and Friday.
Pleterski's fraud trial is expected to continue Friday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Police raid the major pro-opposition Halk TV channel in Turkey
articles.summary: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of an important pro-opposition television station on Wednesdazy, the day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu was set to start his defense against…

image.caption: The police raided Halk TV in the middle of a live broadcast Image: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Wednesday morning, the live broadcast was halted, Halk TV's headquarters in the city of Istanbul were searched, and a new administrator was appointed by the government to run the media outlet. An arrest warrant was issued for the station's CEO, Cafer Mahiroglu, who currently lives in London. According to prosecutors, 11 people were arrested.

Turkey has faced criticism for years over restrictions on press freedom. Halk TV is one of the country's best-known opposition television stations and regularly broadcasts critical reports about Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Justice and Development Party (AKP). After the raid, journalists were initially prevented from entering the building. Pre-recorded programs were broadcast instead of live reports.

The timing is particularly sensitive: Halk TV was raided on the very day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoglu was scheduled to begin his defense against corruption charges in court. The channel has been an important source of information for those following the trial.

Imamoglu, who won the mayoral election in Istanbul in 2019 and remained in office until his arrest on March 19, 2025, is one of Erdogan's most significant rivals, considered a beacon of hope for the opposition. He is still expected to run for president in 2028.

He is accused of establishing and running a criminal organization, as well as of various related financial crimes. Prosecutors are seeking a prison term of 2,352 years related to 142 charges. Imamoglu denies the allegations, arguing that the case is politically motivated.

blocks.caption: 11 people were arrested in conjunction with the raid on Halk TV headquarters Image: ANKA

blocks.text: Raid linked to investigation into Cafer Mahiroglu
Istanbul prosecutors said that the raid on Halk TV was linked to an investigation into its CEO Mahiroglu, who is accused of bribery, bid rigging and money laundering.

They said that arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people, on top of the 11 arrests. Assets belonging to companies allegedly linked to Mahiroglu were also seized and a trustee appointed to run the firms.
The opposition responded with sharp criticism of the police raid. Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the social democratic New Party (Yeni Parti) said it was a dark day for Turkey.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," Mahiroglu said.
"Showing solidarity with Halk TV means supporting the struggle for democracy in Turkey," Ozel said.

He added that "only dictators" would launch "a dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee […]" and criticized the fact that this had occurred on the day that Imamoglu was due to begin his defense.

blocks.caption: Many people in Turkey protested in support of Ekrem Imamoglu when he was jailed in 2025, like here in Izmir on May 19, 2025Image: Berkcan Zengin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Journalists' union slams raid
The Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS) also condemned the raid on the platform X, describing it as arbitrary and arguing that the press was free and should not be censored.

Editor-in-chief Suat Toktas tried in vain to persuade the new state-appointed administrator to continue live broadcasts. In a video released by the TV channel, he said that what was happening was "illegal."
Halk TV began broadcasting on January 10, 2005 and its live broadcasts gained widespread attention particularly during the 2013 Gezi Park protests. Cafer Mahiroglu took over the station in 2020.

articles.summary: National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Thursday said that Vice President Sara Duterte should file a case if she believes that dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. is…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 12:41am

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Thursday said that Vice President Sara Duterte should file a case if she believes that dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. is lying or that he is biased
“Kung may pagsisinungaling silang alegasyon kay Gracioso then file a case. Kung tingin nila ako ay nagiging bias or may mali akong ginagawa, file a case,” he said on Super Radyo dzBB.
(If they have false allegations against Gracioso, then file a case. If they think I am becoming biased or that I am doing something wrong, file a case.)

“Pero 'yung dudulog ka sa media, you will make an appeal on the emotion ng mga tao, magbibigay ng impormasyon na sasakyan ng mga troll para 'yun 'yung gawing atake, hindi 'yun ang katanggap-tanggap na behavior dapat,” he added.
(But if you go to the media, you will appeal to the emotions of the people, provide information that trolls will latch onto to use as an attack; that is not acceptable behavior.)

To recall, Gracioso alleged that he delivered cash to the vice president, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte, and former President Rodrigo Duterte on former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco’s instructions.
She has denied the allegations against her.

Matibag, meanwhile, said that the focus should now be on her alleged “underdeclared” properties.This comes amid the NBI’s probe into the real properties listed in the vice president’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs).
“We are way beyond the affidavit of Gracioso,” he said.
“Ang tanong na ngayon, ano ba itong mga properties na ito. Dineklara mo sa SALN, bakit underdeclared, tapos ngayon sasabihin, hindi ikaw yung may-ari,” he added.
(The question now is, what are these properties? You declared them in your SALN, so why were they underdeclared? Then now you’re saying you’re not the owner.)
Matibag said the investigation has been referred to the Office of the Ombudsman.
Meanwhile, Matibag addressed allegations by Duterte that the NBI was defending Gracioso.

“Well, to a certain extent na sasabihin pinoprotektahan, lahat ng tao, kailangan namin proteksyonan. Pero ano ba yung ibig sabihin ng pinoproteksyunan? Hindi na si Gracioso yung usapan dito, pinag-usapan natin dito, yung mga ari-arian,” Matibag said.

(Well, to a certain extent, when we are saying protection, we need to protect all people. But what does protection even mean? We are not just talking about Gracioso here, but the properties.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat
articles.summary:
Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.

After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.
The spat began on Thursday morning when the Home Office claimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year.

From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped.
It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims.

“Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said.

Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.”
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals.
Mahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.

“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”
The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025.
Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February.
In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum.
Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans.

Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality.

After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers.
India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total.
About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said.
“There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.”
Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”.

The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.”

UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation.
“There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation.
“Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved.

“The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.”
Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record.
“It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.”

Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support.
“It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”

articles.title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’
articles.summary:
Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture

Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that…

blocks.text: Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.

Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.

Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.
Attorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.

According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.
Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”

Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.

Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.

Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.

articles.title: Céline Dion is the latest Barbie doll, but fans quibble over likeness
articles.summary: Already a bestselling recording artist, Grammy and Juno award winner and musical icon, Canadian singer Céline Dion is adding a new accolade to her shelf: Collectible Barbie doll.

image.caption: Céline Dion is the latest famous figure celebrated in Mattel's Barbie Signature line, a series of premium collectible dolls. (Mattel Creations)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Already a bestselling recording artist, Grammy and Juno award winner and musical icon, Canadian singer Céline Dion is adding a new accolade to her shelf: Collectible Barbie doll.
Canadian singer added to Mattel's premium collectible line
Already a bestselling recording artist, Grammy and Juno award winner and musical icon, Céline Dion is adding a new accolade to her shelf: Collectible Barbie doll.
But toymaker Mattel's salute to the famed Canadian singer has rankled some fans, who say the likeness doesn't resemble their queen of the power ballad.

Mattel announced the Dion doll on Monday as part of its Barbie Signature Series, the toy company's premium line of collectible dolls celebrating famous faces from the worlds of fashion, the arts, sport and more.
Previous figures honoured with specialty dolls include Miley Cyrus, Whitney Houston, Marilyn Monroe, Venus and Serena Williams, and Dr. Jane Goodall.
Céline Dion finally gets her very own Barbie doll — and yes, there's a Titanic throwback

Dion's limited edition doll recreates her look from the 1998 Academy Awards, when the historical romance Titanic scored 11 Oscar wins, including best original song for My Heart Will Go On, which the Quebec-born singer performed during the ceremony.
"It is a true honour to join the Barbie legacy with a doll inspired by one of the most meaningful moments of my career," Dion said in a statement.
"I hope this doll inspires everyone to express themselves with confidence, follow their dreams and believe in the power of their own voice."

The doll is based on Dion's look from the 1998 Academy Awards, where she performed My Heart Will Go from the film Titanic and the soaring ballad won the Oscar for best original song. (Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)
A wave of initial fan reactions expressed dismay on social media; though happy with the tribute, they shared disappointment about the likeness of the doll, which retails for $90.

"So sorry but she doesn't look like our Céline," a fan with the username celinedion_amour noted on the Barbie Instagram announcement, offering praise for the "iconic dress and the necklace" but unhappiness with the doll's face.
"Why did you all do Celine like that?!" added commenter duchess_rizzy. "I thought it's old lady Rose from Titanic."
A host of fans gave the doll thumbs down, saying its face did not resemble the Canadian singer. (Barbie/Instagram)

Others noted that rather than Dion, the doll appeared to resemble actress and former Real Housewives of Beverly Hills cast member Lisa Rinna. Others noted a closer resemblance to Catherine, the Princess of Wales.

blocks.text: Recent concert comeback

Last month, Dion made a momentous return to performing in the Parisian suburb of Nanterre at Plenitude Arena, Europe's largest indoor concert venue, where she kicked off a series of more than two dozen highly anticipated shows that will stretch into 2027.
Celine Dion marks triumphant comeback at Paris residency opening
It marked her first concert in six years, following a brief public performance closing out the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

The Grammy and Juno-winning singer had stepped away from the spotlight in 2022 after revealing she'd been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a progressive neurological autoimmune disorder that causes pain, stiffness and muscle spasms.

articles.title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
articles.summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.

blocks.text: "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"

Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".

Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.

Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.

President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".

Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.

That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability
articles.summary: Under Republic Act No. 9442 or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, public ridicule and vilification against PWDs are strictly prohibited.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 12:13am
A podcast show was recently terminated after its hosts made disparaging remarks about Kris Aquino's son, Josh, and his disability.
The network issued a statement apologizing for the remarks in the now-deleted Machong Chismisan post as it garnered an uproar online.
TV Host Boy Abunda condemned the remarks, describing them as cruel and hurtful to Josh and other people with disabilities (PWDs) and their families.

Meanwhile, child protection specialist Ace Diloy told GMA News Online that as much the public enjoys their right to freedom of speech, they should also exercise their humanity and emphasize with the vulnerable sectors.
Under Republic Act No. 9442 or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, public ridicule and vilification against PWDs are strictly prohibited.
The law amended to RA No. 7277 or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons.

RA 9442 defined public ridicule as an "act of making fun or contemptuous initiating or making mockery of persons with disability whether in writing or in words, or in action due to their impairment/s."

"No individual, group or community shall execute any of these acts of ridicule against persons with disability in any time and place which could intimidate or result in loss of self-esteem of the latter," the law stated.
Meanwhile, the amended measure defined vilification as an utterance of slanderous and abusive statements against, or inciting hatred toward or severe ridicule of, a PWD.
"Any individual, group or community is hereby prohibited from vilifying any person with disability which could result into loss of self-esteem of the latter," the law stated.
A person found committing such prohibited acts will face a fine of P5,000 to P100,000 or imprisonment for six months to two years, or both.
Repeat offenders will be fined P100,000 to P200,000 or imprisonment of two to six years, or both.
If the violator is a corporation, organization or any similar entity, its officials directly involved will be liable.
If the violator is a foreigner, they will be deported immediately after serving their prison sentence without further deportation proceedings.

Upon filing a complaint and after proper notice and hearing, authorities may cancel or revoke the business permit, operating permit, franchise, or other privileges of any business that violates the said measure.
— BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Poll: Inflation, corruption top concerns of Pinoys
articles.summary: More than four years into the Marcos administration, reducing the basic cost of goods remains the most urgent concern of most Filipinos, based on a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia.

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 12:00am
Results of the Sept. 17 to 24 survey released yesterday found that 71 percent of the respondents considered inflation as among the three most urgent national concerns of the respondents.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — More than four years into the Marcos administration, reducing the basic cost of goods remains the most urgent concern of most Filipinos, based on a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia.
It went up by 14 percentage points from 57 percent in a similar survey conducted in July.
Reacting to the survey results, Malacañang assured the nation efforts are being made to fight hunger.
“These interventions are continuously being undertaken by the government,” Palace press officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said at a media briefing.

“If some of our countrymen are not yet covered by the assistance of the government, we would want to know where they are located so we can assess the situation, determine what is lacking and identity the assistance we can provide,” she added.
Based on the survey, controlling inflation was ranked first by 36 percent of the respondents, the largest proportion among issues included in the poll.
It was also the issue selected by most respondents across geographic areas and socio-economic classes.
Meanwhile, 39 percent of the respondents identified graft and corruption as among their top three concern. It went down from 43 percent in July.

Other top issues included in the survey were increasing the pay of workers (36 percent), fighting criminality (24 percent), reducing poverty (21 percent), creating more jobs (18 percent), fighting the widespread sale and use of illegal drugs (18 percent) and lowering the price of gasoline (14 percent).

Selected by less than 10 percent of the respondents were issues such as providing assistance to farmers, promoting peace, addressing hunger, equal enforcement of the law, reducing taxes, responding to needs of areas affected by calamities, stopping the destruction of the environment, providing support to small businesses, defending the integrity of Philippine territory, protecting overseas workers and preparing to face any kind of terrorism.
The survey had 2,400 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus two percent.
