articles.title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Russia reports a Ukrainian strike on an oil refinery on Thursday, after Ukraine's president says a pause is over following fresh Russian attacks.

blocks.text: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.

The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said restrictions to Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.
The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

After the unexpected restriction to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection on Tuesday, there were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame. But owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this, suggesting it was the Trump administration's doing. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, referring to the the military-focused version of Starlink.
They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions".

Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.

But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

Ukrainian officials have said they were not warned before a speed limit was imposed on the Starlink uplink, whose sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US Department of Defense (DoD) contract.
Musk wrote on Wednesday that the systems were owned and controlled by the US government and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [Trump]."
The Trump administration has not commented on the issue. The BBC has approached the White House and the DoD for comment.

articles.title: Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live
articles.summary: The US president said that the war will end ‘as soon as I want it to end’ as the midterms take place under a cloud of economic uncertainty

blocks.text: Donald Trump claims Iran war 'will end very soon'

US president Donald Trump claimed the Iran war ‘will end very soon,’ as voters consider their options ahead of midterm elections that are taking place amid economic uncertainty and ongoing global conflict.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday evening, Trump said: “The Iran war will end very soon. It’s going to end very soon, as soon as I want it to end, it’ll end.” He added that Iran would “never have a nuclear weapon” and that oil prices would “drop like a rock”.

The US president has in recent weeks attempted to shift focus towards Ukraine, and has suggested that its attack on Russian refineries are responsible for rising fuel prices. His renewed messaging on Iran suggests that the price of daily goods – and gas at the tank – are having an impact at the polls.

Voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms are increasingly disenchanted with the economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
Elsewhere:

items: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, faced a grilling from undecided voters on a range of issues from Gaza to his faith at a town hall. Something he emphasized was his aspiration to put residents above party allegiance.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt ‘betrayed’ by the US after Ukraine’s military access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite was restricted. The US president has denied that the administration has cut intelligence sharing but Musk suggested on X that the US government was behind the restrictions.
Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing scrutiny over her claims that she’s a lawyer. Zacharia has clarified some of the questions but the big one remains: has she ever passed the bar?

articles.title: School roof collapse in Pakistan's Peshawar kills dozens of students and one teacher
articles.summary: Local authorities said more than 50 other people were injured in the disaster. Roof collapses have become increasingly common in Pakistan.

image.caption: Emergency services were working to clear the rubble, looking for more survivorsImage: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province's Emergency Service/AFP

blocks.text: Officials in Peshawar, Pakistan, confirmed on Thursday that at least 28 pupils under the age of 13 died when an elementary school roof collapsed in the Afridi Abad area of the city.

One teacher has also died, they said. The deceased, along with more than 50 other injured people, were brought to Lady Reading Hospital as rescue workers rushed to clear the rubble and search for more survivors.
"We have taken out ​at ‌least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, but added that more children were thought to still be under the rubble.
From her hospital bed, a teacher told reporters that the school had three floors and more than 1,200 pupils and staff.
The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear.
Roof collapses becoming more regular
Local media in Pakistan noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly routine across the country, due to poor building standards and maintenance.

In July, three young girls were killed near Umerkot when the outer wall of a government school gave way. That same month, one child died and five were injured in Lahore when the roof of an under-construction private school collapsed.
One month earlier, 14 children were killed in a similar manner at a private tutoring facility in Lahore, which came shortly after yet another such incident in Dera Ghazi Khan.

October 15, 2026
Alcohol ban comes into force at all German train stations

blocks.caption: A few dozen stations, including Cologne's main station, imposed the ban much earlier as part of a test phase [FILE: July 23, 2026]Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.
All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones.

Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.
Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train.
Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.

A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.
The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.

"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.

Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.

A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.

articles.title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
articles.summary: Residents have been told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.

blocks.text: Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.
A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.
Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.
Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.
Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.
"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.
He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.
The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.
More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

articles.title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
articles.summary: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
articles.byline: Vanessa Buschschlüter, Mariana Schreiber, Vitor Tavares

blocks.text: Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.
The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.
Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.

Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.
The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.

Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."
The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.
Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.
"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.
Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.
But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.
The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.
The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.
Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.
The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.
"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.
"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

articles.title: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses
articles.summary: Businesses must brace for further risks from transport fares, electricity, wages, El Niño, and a weak peso

blocks.text: September’s 7.2% inflation rate was bad enough on its own. For businesses, the bigger concern is that price pressures could spread beyond the food and fuel shocks that first pushed inflation higher.

Seasonally adjusted inflation accelerated to 1.1% month on month in September from 0.5% in August. In what National Statistician Dennis Mapa described as a relatively “rare” broad increase, 11 of 13 major commodity groups posted faster inflation, while 16 of 18 regions saw inflation pick up. Core inflation also climbed to 4.7%, its highest in three years.

Nerve spoke with three economists to understand whether this is turning into a more persistent inflation problem and what businesses should prepare for heading into 2027. None sees a prolonged second wave as inevitable, but the risk is becoming harder to dismiss.
The September uptick comes as several price increases have yet to fully work their way through the economy. Among them:

items: Recent jeepney, bus, and taxi fare hikes were barely captured by the Philippine Statistics Authority in September and should show up more clearly in October. Passenger transport by road carries a 3.5% weight in the inflation basket.

Meralco has won approval to raise its average distribution rate from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, its first increase after a rate review in 15 years. Once implemented in November, that increases energy costs for households and businesses.
The P60 minimum wage increase in Metro Manila took effect only on September 26, which means possible cost pass-through could be reflected in later months.

El Niño could add another supply shock into early 2027, with economists warning that a strong drought could cut rice and other food production across the Philippines and the region while also putting pressure on power supply and electricity costs.
The weakness of the Philippine peso is another source of inflation, as it raises the peso cost of imported fuel, food, raw materials, and equipment and could keep feeding into domestic prices.

blocks.text: Mapa pointed to energy, transport, and housing rents as some of the harder pressures to unwind. Electricity inflation was already 14.6% in September, while rents rose 4% and carry more than a 12% weight in the consumer price basket.
SM Investments Corporation group economist Robert Dan Roces expects inflation to remain a concern, but said much will depend on food and energy prices over the coming months.
“Some businesses may feel the pressure, but demand should remain relatively resilient,” he told Nerve.

RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort told Nerve that inflation may pick up further in the coming months “in view of second-round inflation effects or higher prices of other affected goods and services, or pass-through effects, especially due to higher minimum wages.”

Meanwhile, Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said a second, stickier wave becomes more plausible if higher food, fuel, electricity, and transport costs begin feeding into other prices and keep inflation expectations elevated.

Agriculture, transport, food businesses, and energy-intensive manufacturing face the most direct exposure, while smaller firms have less room to absorb higher costs. Manufacturing may be especially vulnerable given that the sector was already weakening before the latest inflation pressures intensified, with employment falling to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July and 3.46 million in June.
“Small businesses, meanwhile, have less room to absorb higher costs, and retailers could suffer as households spend more on necessities and cut back elsewhere,” Punongbayan told Rappler.

Even as the “ber” months go by, retailers may need to temper expectations for the usual consumption boost. Consider that inflation among the bottom 30% of households reached 9% in September, compared with 7.2% nationally, leaving lower-income consumers with even less room for discretionary spending.
Forecasts vary considerably on how quickly inflation will ease in 2027, with Ricafort taking the most pessimistic view while institutional forecasts generally cluster between 4% and 5.4%.
High inflation also creates a second problem for businesses through interest rates. Here’s how economists think the BSP will react:

items: Roces expects the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to be more cautious in putting too much additional pressure on growth.

Ricafort is more hawkish, seeing scope for further tightening while inflation remains far above the 2% to 4% target. He also noted that the BSP could partly match future US Federal Reserve hikes to manage interest rate differentials and help stabilize the peso.

Punongbayan said further hikes are possible and easing could be pushed into 2027 depending on how core inflation and expectations go, though higher key policy rates risk further straining borrowing, investment, and growth without fixing supply-side pressures.

blocks.text: The next BSP policy decision is scheduled for October 22, with another Monetary Board meeting set for December 17.
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. articles.title: Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why.
articles.summary: Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

image.caption: Around 60% of the Amazon rainforest is within Brazil's bordersImage: Paralaxis/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are few national elections that carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.
Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.
"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.
"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."
One of nature's most powerful defenses
The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

blocks.caption: Parts of the Amazon rainforest have been burned down to make way for cattle farms.Image: Andre Penner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.
During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank, Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.
Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.
Pitting environment against the economy

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.
"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest'," said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Centre at London-based think tank Chatham House.
"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

blocks.caption: Thousands of students have marched in Rio de Janiero protesting against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro as president following the first round of electionsImage: Mariana Greif/JNA PRESS/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.
"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.
More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.
In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.
No straightforward climate success story

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

blocks.caption: Storing vast amounts of CO2, the Amazon rainforest is often referred to as the lung of the Earth Image: AP

blocks.text: Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".
"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25th. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians, climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon, to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.
"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

articles.title: SC applicants weigh in on raising qualifications of nat'l candidates
articles.summary: The final batch of applicants vying for the Supreme Court (SC) position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier on Thursday weighed in on increasing the qualifications required…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 5:39pm

The final batch of applicants vying for the Supreme Court (SC) position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier on Thursday weighed in on increasing the qualifications required for national elective positions in government.

For the second batch, Commission on Audit (COA) chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba, Government Corporate Counsel Solomon Hermosura, lawyer German Lichauco II, and Commission on Elections Commissioner Ernesto Maceda faced the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC).
Lichauco said that amending the Constitution was "long overdue."

"By putting up the bar, we will be able to weed out the possible candidates who are not qualified for such position. By raising the bar, upgrading the qualification, then we are now being given a greater position to choose wisely," he said.

"Fortunately, unfortunately… our electoral system is based on popularity and because of that, certain individuals who may not even be qualified for certain positions are elected simply because the masses see, the masses know of them, and the masses think that what they see is actually the person they are voting," he said.
Lichauco said that with more qualifications, the public has a better opportunity to choose wisely.

Under the 1987 Constitution, individuals seeking to be president, vice president, senator, and congressman must be a natural-born citizen and must be literate while each position has a varying requirement on age and residency in the country.
Cordoba also said he was in favor of increasing the qualifications.

"Because the complexity of governance is quite different right now. We're governing around 120 million people and the needs and the wants and the desires are different from maybe 10, 5, 20 years ago," he said.
"So the demands on the candidates, on the executive elected officials are quite high (so) I agree with that," he added.
However, Cordoba stressed that the qualifications cannot be amended simply through judicial legislation.
"It has to go through a constitutional charter change," he said.
Meanwhile, Maceda and Hermosura believe that there is no need to raise the qualifications.
"I am more comfortable with lesser qualification than with more," Maceda said.
"That's more democratic. It allows more participation and it does not impose limitations," he added.
According to Maceda, the right of people to vote and the right to run for public office should be given equal weight.

"The popular position nowadays are to require educational, to demand educational requirements. Unless it is shown that that's a guarantee of better service, then I don't see how that should supplant the existing order," he said.
Hermosura, meanwhile, said he was not in favor of too many qualifications, saying that in the private sector, the focus is on past performance and not on qualifications.
He also expressed hope that raising qualifications for national elective positions will not restrict access to public service.
He said that sometimes, meeting the qualifications requires a certain degree of financial stability.

The JBC panel was composed of Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Batangas Representative Gerville Luistro, former Supreme Court associate justice Jose Catral Mendoza, Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Erlinda Piñera Uy, lawyer Nesauro Hernandez Firme, and lawyer Jose Mejia.
Lazaro-Javier is set to restire on November 16, 2026. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
articles.summary: From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals…

image.caption: As technologies become more embedded in daily life, policymakers are weighing the benefits against concerns over data security and foreign influenceImage: Benjamin Bathke/DW

blocks.text: Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?
At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.
The main culprit? Chinese competition.
GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

blocks.caption: GoPro was saved from bankruptcy in September after failed product bets and competition from smartphones have contributed to its declineImage: Christian Ohde/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.
"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.
China's growing tech lead

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.
Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.
"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."
This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.
So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

blocks.caption: Joey Cheng, founder of Prolo Ring, which makes rings that let consumers control remotes and other devices with only their thumbsImage: Benjamin Bathke/DW

blocks.text: Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.
While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."
Privacy and security concerns persist
Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.
A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.
Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

blocks.caption: Xreal, a Chinese smart glasses maker, recently entered the European market through retailers like the UK's Currys in an attempt to grow consumer trust Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.
In addition to privacy concerns, Chinese consumer tech firms have come under scrutiny over espionage and other risks, most recently regarding connected devices like EVs.
Is a new trade war brewing?

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.
A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.
"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.
European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."
China's robot revolution leaves Hong Kong playing catch-up
Can Western companies compete?
As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.
Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.
"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.
To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.
"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.
"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

articles.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
articles.summary: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as global investors fret over potential interest rate hikes

blocks.text: An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in ChatGPT owner OpenAI.
The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, logging its worst performance since July.

The sell-off comes after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher than expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.
The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.
“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid, said.

Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”

The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said earlier this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk.
after newsletter promotion

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.

The latest jitters hit China, where Shanghai’s CSI 300 slipped as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.

European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.
In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

articles.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 34 children and teacher
articles.summary:
Another three pupils from al-Khair school in Peshawar in critical condition after search for survivors

At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school…

blocks.text: At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northern Pakistani city ⁠of Peshawar.
As panicked parents ​and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble.

Most of the victims were under 13 years old ⁠and from low-income households. At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, the regional director of emergency services.
Television footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to ⁠waiting ambulances as people crowded the alley where the school stood.

The roof of a higher floor collapsed on to classrooms below, crumpling two ​storeys of the building, a rescue official said. “The fatalities include ‌12 girl students and a female teacher,” said the Lady ‌Reading hospital spokesperson, Mohammad Asim. Three children remained in critical condition with head injuries, while most of the injured taken to the hospital ‌had been treated and discharged, he added.

The incident took place at 8.48am local time (0348 GMT) and the rescue operation lasted for four to five hours, Khattak said. “It was a weak building structure,” said the Peshawar police chief, Mian Saeed. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse.”
Saeed said the school’s owner had been arrested and an investigation launched. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.

blocks.caption: Mourners attend funeral prayers for children who died in the roof collapse. Photograph: Maaz Awan/AP

blocks.text: Distraught relatives accused the school of ignoring concerns about ‌the building’s condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.

The ​school was located in a poor, crowded neighbourhood of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Pakistan’s president imposed a state of emergency on Sunday, saying the provincial government had failed to tackle Islamist militancy from neighbouring Afghanistan, an allegation it denied.
Pakistan spends less than 1% of its approximately $450bn (£340bn) GDP on education, leaving many families dependent on low-cost private schools.

Many of those schools operate from poorly maintained rented buildings with limited oversight, contributing to recurring safety concerns. In June, at least ⁠14 children died when the roof of a tutoring centre housed in a dilapidated building collapsed in the ​eastern city of Lahore.
There was no immediate comment ​from school officials.
The country’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, expressed ​sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims’ families, his office said.

Jawad Ahmad, whose son and daughter survived the incident, said the ‌news had left him devastated. “It felt ​as if someone had shot ​me in the chest when I learned that the school building had collapsed,” he said.

The province, governed for years by the party of the jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, has frequently been at odds with the federal administration. Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, imposed a new governor on the province when he declared the state of emergency on Sunday, sharpening the tensions.

articles.title: PCC slaps onion cartel with record fine of P1.76B
articles.summary: Among those fined is 'onion queen' Lilia Cruz, the alleged cartel mastermind. It's the biggest fine ever imposed by the Philippine Competition Commission.

blocks.text: ONIONS. A market vendor arranges large onions imported from China which sell for P350/kilo at Libertad Market in Pasay City on January 17, 2023.
Rappler
Among those fined is 'onion queen' Lilia Cruz, the alleged cartel mastermind. It's the biggest fine ever imposed by the Philippine Competition Commission.

items: The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) imposed a P1.76-billion fine on members of an onion cartel involved in illegal market allocation and manipulation of onion prices.
The cartel's activities included collusion in importation and distribution, controlling nearly 50% of onion import clearances in 2020 and 2021, leading to a significant price surge in late 2022.
Key individuals and firms were identified and fined, while the PCC emphasized its commitment to combating anti-competitive practices and protecting consumers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Almost four years since the country’s onion crisis, the Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) imposed a combined P1.76-billion fine against onion cartel members that colluded in an “illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage, and wholesale distribution of red and yellow onions.”
In late 2022, onion prices in the Philippines skyrocketed to over P800 per kilo, prompting a House probe into alleged price manipulation and cartel operations.

“Because the importers’ submitted audited financial statements were found to be grossly understated, the Commission computed the fines using actual import clearance volumes, and wholesale prices reported by the Philippine Statistics Authority,” the PCC said on Thursday, October 15.
This comes two years after the PCC sued onion firms in 2024, as well as a dawn raid of warehouses in September 2023, including the respondents’ offices located in Golden Shine Corporate Center.

“An examination of the evidence [from the raid] revealed that Golden Shine systematically applied for sanitary and phytosanitary import clearances using the other respondent-importers’ credentials, assigned the same importers as consignees, monitored permit allocations, and coordinated shipments. By accumulating permits across separate corporate entities, the respondents collectively controlled nearly 50 percent of all approved import clearances for red and yellow (or white) onions in 2020 and 2021, routing imported shipments to cold storage facilities managed under Tian Long [Corp.] from where imported onions were distributed nationwide,” the PCC explained.
Six firms named engaged in the onion cartel and subsequently fined are:

items: Golden Shine International Freight Forwarders Corp.
Tian Long Corp.
La Reina Fresh Vegetables & Young Indoor Plants, Inc.
Yom Trading Corp.
Vegefru Producing Store
Rosal Fruit and Vegetable Trading

blocks.text: In 2024, the Department of Agriculture blacklisted importers linked to the cartel: La Reina Fresh Vegetables Young Indoor Plants Incorporate, Vegefru Producing Store, and Yom Trading Corporation.
The individual officers held liable are:

items: Lilia Cruz, president of Golden Shine
Eric Pabilona, corporate executive officer of Golden Shine and corporate secretary of Tian Long
Renato Francisco Jr., chairman and president of La Reina and Yom Trading
Letty Baculando, incorporator of Golden Shine

blocks.text: According to the PCC, charges against other companies allegedly involved — Philippine Vieva Group of Companies, Inc. and the Vegetable Importers, Exporters & Vendors Association of the Philippines Inc. — were dismissed due to “insufficient evidence.”

But key officers of these companies are also the same individual officers fined, as mentioned above such as Cruz and Pabilona. Cruz had been referred to as the “onion queen” or “Mrs. Sibuyas” for being implicated as the cartel mastermind.

“By imposing the maximum fines, the PCC underscores its commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct,” PCC Executive Director Kenneth Tanate said.
The government initially sought a P2.423-billion fine against the cartel back in 2024.
Aside from the fines, those involved in cartel activities may also face criminal liability if the Department of Justice-Office for Competition finds basis in filing cases.
The PCC is the quasi-judicial body that implements Republic Act No. 10667 or the Philippine Competition Act, which seeks to promote and protect market competition in the country. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
articles.summary: The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October.

blocks.text: Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.
An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections.
"Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.
Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.
Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.
But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.
The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".
Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.
He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.
Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.
The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.

On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges.
"Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.

The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India".
Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest.
"I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.
He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.
Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters.

He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.

Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call.
On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.
On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

articles.title: Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's OM in a political tangle
articles.summary: Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

image.caption: Sheikh Mansour, Manchester City's owner, is popular enough for one fan to dress up as himImage: Oli Scarff/AFP

blocks.text: Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.
City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.
Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

blocks.caption: Players like Erling Haaland may be forced to leave if City's punishment is severImage: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: "I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in non-league, so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."
Tarnished trophies?

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.
UAE links have Burnham on back foot

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has faced increasing scrutiny over his relationship with the UAEImage: Phil Noble/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.
UAE build where others can't
Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

blocks.caption: Sheikh Mansour is Manchester City's owner but is rarely seen at gamesImage: Martin Rickett/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: "A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."
State-owned clubs starting to think smart despite concerns

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

blocks.caption: Paris Saint-Germain have become the team to beat in EuropeImage: Franck Fife/AFP

blocks.text: There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

articles.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
articles.summary:
At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports

Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are…

blocks.text: Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

blocks.caption: Protesters call for a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in February in Senegal’s capital, Dakar. The issue was promoted as a national priority in elections. Photograph: Zohra Bensemra/Reuters

blocks.text: Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Martin Romualdez remains detained in Payatas jail
articles.summary: The lawmaker is still in detention at the New Quezon City Jail for his multibillion-peso plunder case tied to the flood control controversy

blocks.text: Claim: Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez is not in detention and is now out of the country.
Rating: FALSE
Why we fact-checked this: Facebook page Makata Ng Bayan posted the claim on October 14, 2026. As of writing, it has reached over 4,700 reactions, 1,600 shares, and 700 comments.
The post included a photo of Romualdez with his cousin, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and text labeling it as “breaking news.”
The graphic reads: “Breaking News! Martin Romualdez wala na sa kulungan nakalabas na ng Bansa! Si Marcos naman habang sabog ay naging tuta ng sindikato Kaya dapat ng lumayas at Palayasin.”
(Breaking news! Martin Romualdez is no longer in jail; he has left the country! As for Marcos, he became the puppet of a syndicate while high on drugs, so he should leave and be ousted.)

The post received mixed views in the comments section. Some criticized the Marcos administration for allowing Romualdez to flee the country, while others questioned the post’s credibility for calling for a revolt against the government.

The facts: Romualdez has been detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14, 2026. He was arrested over a P7.44-billion plunder case related to the flood control scandal on September 7.
The Ombudsman dubbed Romualdez a “central figure” in the scheme due to his strong influence in Congress during his time as House speaker.
His transfer to the jail was not immediately carried out after his arrest, as he was first confined at a hospital in San Juan City hours before the warrant against him was served.
In his arraignment before the Sandiganbayan on September 16, Romualdez pleaded not guilty.
His bail hearing began on October 12, and will continue every Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday. Meanwhile, the presentation of evidence for his case is set to begin on November 23.
Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously debunked false claims revolving around the lawmaker.
